notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material on this chapter. I didn't find enough to fill in every part of your brief, so here's what's missing:

- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I didn't find anything on Jeremiah 27 from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace:** I found no teaching from these movements on this chapter.
- **Differences between traditions:** None of the pages I read set out a Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran or Anglican position on this chapter. What I can offer instead is that older commentators from different traditions sometimes disagree, mostly about v. 1, v. 7 and v. 11. Labels such as "Reformed", "Baptist" and "Methodist" below are my own notes, not something the pages say.
- **Gaps:** I found nothing specific on vv. 4, 13, 14, 20 or 21 beyond general summaries, so I've grouped those with nearby verses.

---

**v. 1**
- **The date problem.** Most Hebrew manuscripts say "Jehoiakim" here, but v. 3 names Zedekiah. Enduring Word (Guzik) calls "Jehoiakim" a problem, because it isn't in many manuscripts and doesn't match with the rest of the chapter… This is a likely scribal error. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/
- **Clarke (Methodist):** the prophecy came about the fourth year of ZEDEKIAH, and not Jehoiakim, as in the text. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-1.html
- **Calvin (Reformed) disagrees.** He takes the date as written: God gave Jeremiah this prophecy under Jehoiakim but did not design it to be immediately promulgated (meaning it wasn't to be announced yet). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-1.html
- **Lightfoot's middle way:** Jeremiah was ordered to make these yokes in Jehoiakim's time to signify the subjection of Judah to the king of Babylon, but that he was ordered to send them to foreign kings in the reign of Zedekiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-1.html
- **Gill (Baptist)** leans the same way and calls this most probable. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv/jeremiah/27-1.html
- **Poole rejects the copying-error theory**, saying it is dangerous to admit that. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-1.htm
- **Keil and Delitzsch** answer the objection that the fourth of eleven years is hardly the "beginning": the idea of beginning is relative… The reign of Zedekiah is divided into two halves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-1.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET notes, quoted on Precept Austin):** the verse has long been recognized as textually corrupt, and the Greek Old Testament (LXX) leaves the whole verse out. The NET dates the event to 594/3 BC and points to the Babylonian Chronicles, which record uprisings Nebuchadnezzar had just put down. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-27-commentary
- **Lineage note:** Bible Hub's study note contrasts godly Josiah with his son, who did evil. It says this reminds readers that lineage alone cannot guarantee faithfulness. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/27-1.htm

**v. 2**
- **A real yoke.** The yoke was a wooden bar fastened to an animal's neck with leather straps. Feinberg (quoted by Guzik) says Jeremiah really wore it in public, since Hananiah broke it (28:10–11). Guzik's summary of what the yoke said: "I'm the boss. You work for me. I regard you as a beast of burden." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/
- **Gill** thinks Jeremiah wore the yokes not all of them together, but one after another, at different times, so that people would ask what they meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-2.html
- **Walton (IVP)** notes that Assyrian carvings show captives wearing such yokes. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-27-commentary

**v. 3**
- **Why the envoys were there.** They had come to plan a revolt with Zedekiah. Jeremiah probably spoke to them while wearing the yokes. Thompson says Babylon was then in trouble, facing attacks from Elam and a revolt in Syria. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/
- **One yoke or several?** Coffman says five yokes were made and actually sent to the five kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-2.html Harrison thinks only one yoke was made and the nations were sent word of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/ Utley thinks the "them" in v. 3 probably… refers to a message, not a yoke. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-27-commentary
- **Matthew Henry** pictures Jeremiah giving each envoy a yoke for his king, as they left with their treaty signed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-11.html

**vv. 4–5**
- **God as Creator.** Utley reads v. 5 as a claim that the LORD made the world and rules over every nation. The phrase "great power and outstretched arm" is also used of the Exodus. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-27
- **Matthew Henry:** God gives land and power to whomever he pleases. He adds that Dominion is not founded in grace (power isn't a sign of God's favour). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_027.cfm
- **Calvin** says v. 4 tells the ambassadors to report to their masters that they must all accept Babylon's yoke. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-27.html

**v. 6**
- **"My servant."** Ryken (quoted by Guzik) says this is the kind of language an ancient king would use to describe one of his vassals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/
- **Calvin:** the title doesn't mean God counted Nebuchadnezzar as one of his own people. It was said so that the nations would understand that bowing to Babylon was obeying God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-27.html
- **Utley** lists the Bible's uses of "my servant." Nebuchadnezzar falls in the group of unbelieving rulers, like Cyrus, who serve God's purposes. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-27
- **The wild animals:** Kingcomments says these are mentioned to show how far Nebuchadnezzar's authority reached (compare Daniel 2:38). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-27.html

**v. 7**
- **Traditional reading.** The son is Evil-merodach and the grandson Belshazzar. Clarke, quoted by Guzik, says this was All which was literally fulfilled. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/
- **Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown** explain that two kings in between (Neriglissar and his son) weren't in the direct male line, so the prophecy still holds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-7.htm
- **Cambridge Bible disagrees.** Read literally, it says, the verse is at variance with history, unless it only means that Babylon wouldn't go away quickly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-7.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary** says the verse makes sense only if the "seventy years" is a round number. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-7.htm
- **Coffman** takes the phrase as a general one meaning Nebuchadnezzar and all his successors. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-6.html
- **Utley (modern):** the LXX leaves out "grandson," and the phrase is a literary way of asserting Babylon's domination for a period of time. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-27
- **Ellicott** says the words cut both ways. They warn the nations not to resist, and they warn the king not to think his dynasty will last. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-7.htm

**v. 8**
- **Precept Austin:** refusing to submit is not merely political resistance but rebellion against God's sovereign decree. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-27-commentary
- **Benson:** Nebuchadnezzar acted unjustly, but God allowed it to punish the nations' idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-7.htm

**vv. 9–10**
- **The forbidden advisers.** Utley explains each term: diviners, dreamers, soothsayers and sorcerers. All are banned in Deuteronomy 18:9–14. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-27
- **Guzik:** like Judah, the neighbouring kings had their own prophets promising that Babylon would be turned back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/
- **Calvin** discusses whether the false prophets' words mean "You will not serve" (a prediction) or "Do not serve" (a command), and keeps the first. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-27.html

**v. 11**
- **Submission means staying home.** Nations that submit avoid exile. Keil and Delitzsch explain that conquerors only destroyed and deported peoples who resisted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-11.htm
- **A word play.** The same Hebrew root means both "serve" and "till." Calvin's summary: serve the king of Babylon, and the land will serve you. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-11.htm
- **Calvin** also says the warning was really aimed at the Jews. If God would spare pagan nations, how much more his own people? https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-27.html
- **Applying it today.** F. B. Meyer applies the verse to accepting God's discipline. Guzik contrasts this yoke with Christ's easy yoke (Matthew 11:29). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/ The Bible Hub study note links the verse to Romans 13:1. https://biblehub.com/study/jeremiah/27-11.htm

**vv. 12–15**
- **To the king.** Precept Austin sees three commands here: submit, serve, live. Together they call Zedekiah to humble himself under God's discipline. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-27-commentary
- **Matthew Henry:** the king's decision would settle the people's fate, so Jeremiah speaks to him as if to all of them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-22.html
- **v. 15:** Utley notes that "I have not sent them" also appears in 23:21 and 29:9. He wonders whether the false prophets believed they were sent. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-27

**vv. 16–17**
- **The false promise.** The prophets promised that the temple articles taken earlier (2 Kings 24:13) would soon come back. Ellicott says the people missed these treasures, and the prophets soothed them with predictions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-16.htm
- **Calvin:** the word "soon" made the lie more convincing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-16.html
- **Cambridge Bible** says the priests had sided with the false prophets. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-16.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** "shortly" was a lie, but "at length" was true. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-17.html

**v. 18**
- **A test for the prophets.** Guzik compares it to Elijah's test of the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the false prophets had neglected one of a prophet's main jobs, praying for the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-18.htm
- **Geneva Bible notes:** true prophets prayed for the people, but these men couldn't, because God had said the opposite. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-18.htm

**vv. 19–21**
- **What was left.** These are the bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz, the bronze "Sea" (a huge basin) and the stands (1 Kings 7). Ellicott thinks the first raid took only the smaller, portable vessels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-19.htm
- **Calvin:** they are named so that people would know nothing would be left remaining in the Temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-19.html
- **Modern note:** the LXX has a much shorter version of vv. 19–22. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/27-18.htm

**v. 22**
- **Fulfilled.** Clarke says the prophecy came true literally (Jeremiah 52:17–23; 2 Kings 25:13). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/27-22.html
- **Restored.** The articles came back under Cyrus (Ezra 1:7–11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-27/
- **Matthew Henry:** We are apt to set our clock before God's dial (we expect things on our schedule rather than God's). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_027.cfm
- **Bible Hub Q&A** sees the vessels' return as foreshadowing restoration in Christ, the true temple. https://biblehub.com/q/Context_of_Jeremiah_27_16_temple_vessels.htm
